## When "Where Is Our Data?" Stalls a Global Rollout

Picture a workplace experience team that's chosen one platform to standardize room booking, events, and catering across offices in Chicago, London, Frankfurt, and Singapore. Three weeks before contract signature, IT security sends back a questionnaire asking where booking data, visitor logs, and backups will physically live, and the deal stops. The culprit is data residency requirements: the legal, regulatory, or contractual rules that dictate the geographic location where an organization's data is stored and processed. The facilities team picked the platform for its features, but procurement, legal, and IT will judge it on where data sits, who can access it, and under which country's laws, and most teams don't find that out until the review is already underway. Here's how residency differs from sovereignty and localization, what the rules look like by region, what workplace platforms specifically need to account for, and the exact questions to put in your RFP.

## Key Takeaways

- Residency, sovereignty, and localization are different obligations, and mixing them up produces the wrong requirements list.
- GDPR regulates transfers out of the EEA rather than mandating EU-only hosting.
- Workplace platforms hold sensitive employee and visitor data, so legal will scrutinize them early.
- Backups, logs, support access, subprocessors, and AI features all count toward residency, not just primary storage.
- Contract language, not marketing claims, is what you can actually hold a vendor to.

## Residency, Sovereignty, and Localization Aren't the Same Thing

These three terms get used interchangeably in vendor questionnaires, and the confusion leads teams to over-require things the law doesn't demand or under-require things it does.

### Data Residency

- Data residency is the physical or geographic location where data is stored, usually chosen by the organization for regulatory, contractual, or policy reasons.
- Choosing an EU hosting region for European employees' booking data is a residency decision.

### Data Sovereignty

- Data sovereignty means data is subject to the laws of the country where it's located, and sometimes also to the laws of the country where the vendor is headquartered.
- That's why EU data stored in Frankfurt by a US-owned provider can still raise questions under the US CLOUD Act, which is why it shows up in reviews of a vendor's [data security and compliance standards](https://gomomentus.com/blog/data-security-compliance-standards).

### Data Localization

- Data localization is the strictest form: a legal mandate that certain data must stay inside a country's borders, often with limits or approval requirements before it can be transferred out.
- China's PIPL and Saudi Arabia's PDPL are common examples.
- Here's the thing: most organizations face residency and sovereignty questions, while far fewer face true localization mandates. Knowing which one applies keeps your requirements list accurate.

## Why Workplace and Space Data Gets Extra Scrutiny

Workplace and event platforms hold more personal data than most teams realize. Room bookings show who met with whom and when. Desk reservations and occupancy sensors show where an employee was during the day, and visitor management logs capture names, companies, and sometimes ID scans of people who don't even work for you. In an [integrated workplace management system](https://gomomentus.com/blog/integrated-workplace-management-system), all of that lives in one place. Integrations widen the footprint further, since every connection to access control systems (PACS), badge readers, IoT occupancy sensors, HR systems, and calendars like Outlook is another place personal data moves and can be stored or logged. That's why [event software integrations](https://gomomentus.com/blog/event-software-integrations) deserve their own line in any security review.

Regulators also treat employee location and movement data as privacy-sensitive. Under GDPR, large-scale monitoring of employees typically calls for a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA), along with clear retention limits and data minimization, such as reporting occupancy in aggregate instead of by named individual wherever your [workplace analytics](https://gomomentus.com/blog/workplace-analytics) allow it. That's the catch with enterprise space management software. The same data that powers [space utilization analytics](https://gomomentus.com/blog/space-utilization-analytics) is the data legal will ask about first. So residency belongs in the evaluation from day one, not as a final-stage checkbox.

## Data Residency Requirements by Region

Data residency requirements vary widely by jurisdiction, and a global workplace portfolio usually has to satisfy several sets of rules at once.

### European Union and United Kingdom

- GDPR doesn't require EU-only hosting. It regulates transfers outside the European Economic Area (EEA), which need an [adequacy decision](https://commission.europa.eu/law/law-topic/data-protection/international-dimension-data-protection/adequacy-decisions_en) (such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework for certified US companies), Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), or Binding Corporate Rules.
- The 2020 Schrems II ruling invalidated Privacy Shield and requires transfer impact assessments when data leaves the EU. Meta's [€1.2 billion fine in 2023](https://www.edpb.europa.eu/news/news/2023/12-billion-euro-fine-facebook-result-edpb-binding-decision_en) for EU-US transfers shows what's at stake.
- The UK follows UK GDPR, using the [International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA) or the UK Addendum](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/international-transfers/) to the SCCs.

### United States

- There's no federal residency mandate for most private-sector data. State privacy laws like California's [CCPA/CPRA](https://oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa) govern how data is handled, not where it lives.
- Sector rules add requirements: HIPAA for health data, and [FedRAMP](https://www.fedramp.gov/) authorization for cloud services used by federal agencies. Some state and public university contracts also require US-only hosting.
- The CLOUD Act lets US authorities request data from US-based providers regardless of where it's stored, which is the core sovereignty concern for non-US buyers.

### Canada

- PIPEDA doesn't require in-country storage, but it holds organizations accountable for personal information sent abroad.
- Quebec's Law 25 requires a privacy impact assessment before personal information leaves the province.

### Asia-Pacific

- Australia's Privacy Act (APP 8) and Singapore's PDPA allow cross-border transfers as long as the receiving party provides comparable protection.
- China's PIPL is a true localization regime for critical information infrastructure operators and high-volume processors, with security assessments required before export.
- India's DPDP Act permits transfers except to countries the government specifically restricts.

### Middle East

- Saudi Arabia's PDPL restricts transfers outside the Kingdom to specific conditions.
- The UAE's federal PDPL and the separate DIFC and ADGM free-zone regimes each have their own transfer rules, so a single "Middle East" policy rarely holds up.

Treat this as a starting map, not legal advice, and confirm specifics with counsel.

## Residency Has to Cover More Than Primary Storage

A vendor can truthfully say "your data is hosted in the EU" while copies, logs, and access paths sit somewhere else entirely, and that gap is where most vendor reviews turn up problems.

### 1: Backups and Disaster Recovery

Backup copies and DR replicas need to stay in the same region or an approved secondary region. Ask for RPO (recovery point objective) and RTO (recovery time objective) commitments in writing, plus the location of the failover site.

### 2: Logs and Telemetry

Application logs, audit trails, and monitoring data often contain names, email addresses, and IP addresses. They're also frequently shipped to a centralized logging tool in another country, which quietly turns a hosting decision into a data transfer.

### 3: Support Access

Residency means little if a support engineer on another continent can view production data. Confirm where support staff are located and whether their access is just-in-time, logged, and approved by you.

### 4: Subprocessors

Every third-party service the vendor uses, from email delivery to analytics to payment processing, is a potential transfer. Require a published subprocessor list and advance notice of changes.

### 5: AI and Analytics Features

Generative AI and machine learning features may send prompts or records to a model hosted outside your region. As [AI integrations with event tools](https://gomomentus.com/blog/ai-integrations-with-event-tools) become standard, ask where AI processing happens, whether customer data is used for training, and whether AI features can be turned off by region.

### 6: Integrations and Data Exports

Data synced to calendars, HR systems, ERPs, and BI tools inherits the residency of wherever it lands. Map your full [event tech stack](https://gomomentus.com/blog/event-tech-stack), because the platform's region is only half the picture.

## Comparing Hosting Models for Residency

You can meet residency through several hosting models, and each one trades cost and speed of deployment against control.

| Hosting Model | How Residency Works | Best For | Tradeoffs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Multi-tenant SaaS in a chosen region | The customer selects a cloud region (for example, an AWS region in Europe) at setup, and data is stored there. | Most corporate and campus portfolios | Shared infrastructure, so confirm logical separation, backups, and support access stay in-region. |
| Single-tenant cloud | A dedicated instance runs in a chosen region. | Organizations with strict isolation or customer-managed key requirements | Higher cost and slower upgrades. |
| Sovereign or government cloud | Infrastructure is operated in-country, sometimes by local entities, to limit foreign legal access. | Public sector and regulated industries | Limited vendor availability and premium pricing. |
| On-premises or private cloud | The organization hosts the software itself. | Rare cases with strict localization mandates | The organization owns patching, uptime, security, and DR, which usually costs more than it saves. |

For most global workplace teams, in-region multi-tenant SaaS from a vendor with strong contractual commitments covers residency without the cost of dedicated infrastructure, and it's the model worth testing first when you compare [enterprise facility management software](https://gomomentus.com/blog/enterprise-facility-management-software).

## The Security Controls That Should Come With Residency

Storing data in the right country doesn't protect it on its own, and IT security reviewers will expect these baseline controls alongside any residency commitment.

- **Identity and Access:** SSO through providers like Okta or Microsoft Entra ID, MFA, automated user provisioning and deprovisioning (SCIM), and least-privilege, role-based permissions. That last piece matters when campus partners, vendors, and student workers all touch the same system.
- **Encryption:** TLS in transit and AES-256 at rest are the standard, with customer-managed keys as an option for organizations that want control over who can decrypt data.
- **Independent Assurance:** A current SOC 2 Type II report and ISO 27001 certification are the baseline, with ISO 27701 (privacy), ISO 27017 and 27018 (cloud security and cloud privacy), and TISAX for automotive clients as useful additional signals.
- **Secure Integrations:** Mutual TLS (mTLS) or scoped API tokens should protect connections to PACS, IoT sensors, and visitor management systems, with logging on every connection.
- **Monitoring and Incident Response:** Look for centralized security logging, defined breach notification timelines (GDPR requires notifying regulators within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach), and a documented incident response plan that fits into your broader approach to [enterprise risk management](https://gomomentus.com/blog/what-is-enterprise-risk-management).

## Questions to Ask Vendors About Data Residency Requirements

Contractual commitments matter more than marketing claims, so turn your data residency requirements into specific RFP questions with answers you can hold the vendor to. It's one of the most useful [steps to making venue technology decisions](https://gomomentus.com/blog/five-steps-to-making-venue-technology-decisions) you can take before signature.

### 1: Which Hosting Regions Can We Choose, and Can Different Sites Use Different Regions?

This matters most for portfolios that span the EU, North America, and APAC, where one region rarely fits every site.

### 2: Where Do Backups, DR Replicas, and Logs Live?

Ask for the answer in writing, not on a call. A verbal "it stays in-region" won't help in an audit.

### 3: Where Are Support Staff Located, and How Is Their Access Controlled and Logged?

You want named locations and an access approval process, not a vague reference to global support.

### 4: Who Are Your Subprocessors, and How Will You Notify Us of Changes?

Notice should arrive before a new subprocessor goes live, with time for you to object.

### 5: Which Transfer Mechanisms Do You Use (SCCs, DPF, IDTA)?

Ask for a signed Data Processing Agreement (DPA) that includes them.

### 6: Where Do AI Features Process Our Data, and Is It Used for Model Training?

If the vendor can't answer clearly, that's an answer in itself.

### 7: What Happens to Our Data at Contract End?

Look for export formats, deletion timelines, and a deletion certificate.

Here's a short sample clause you can adapt:

"Provider shall store and process Customer Personal Data, including backups and disaster recovery copies, solely within \[Region\], and shall not transfer or permit remote access to such data from outside \[Region\] without Customer's prior written consent."

Have legal counsel review any clause language before you use it.

## Residency Doesn't End at Signature

Vendors change subprocessors, open new regions, and add AI features after the contract is signed, so residency needs ongoing checks rather than a one-time review. Build audit rights into the agreement, along with contractual notice before any change to data location. Then schedule an annual review of the vendor's SOC 2 report and subprocessor list. Test the exit plan before you need it, too. Run a sample export to confirm data comes out complete and usable, and confirm the deletion process and timeline at contract end. Good [workplace management software](https://gomomentus.com/blog/workplace-management-software) should make both of those steps routine instead of a scramble.

## How Momentus Keeps Workplace Data Where It Belongs

Every section above points to the same tension. Workplace teams need one standardized system across every building and region, while legal and IT need data to stay in specific places under specific rules. Too often, teams settle it by running a different tool per region, which breaks the portfolio-level visibility they were after in the first place. Put simply, data residency requirements are much easier to meet when region selection is part of standard setup rather than a custom engineering project.
